title: How fires in Indonesia are impacting Singapore’s air
description:
Singapore’s got a reputation for being one of world’s cleanest cities. But right now, it’s covered in a thick blanket of smog. And it’s recently seen its worst air quality levels for the year. The reason? Fires in nearby Indonesia.

Indonesia’s seen its worst wildfire season in years. Huge areas of land have been burning for weeks. Fires are sometimes lit as a way to illegally clear land to make room for plantations - a process known as ‘slash and burn’. Hot and dry conditions caused by extreme weather mean the fires grow and spread easily.

We hear from people in Singapore and Indonesia about how the fires and resulting haze are affecting their daily lives. Plus, BBC reporters Tessa Wong in Singapore and Liza Tambunan in Indonesia explain how both countries are responding.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討印尼野火引發的嚴重跨境煙霾對新加坡及周邊東南亞國家的衝擊。由於非法「刀耕火種」砍伐清地，加上超級 El Niño 現象引發的乾旱，印尼蘇門答臘與加里曼丹爆發自 2015 年以來最嚴重的野火，導致逾 17 萬例急性呼吸道感染。煙霾擴散至新加坡與馬來西亞，造成能見度下降、學校停課，民眾被迫改變日常作息。 BBC 記者 Liza Tambunan 與 Tessa Wong 指出，新加坡政府提供社區中心避難房並發放口罩，但其《跨境煙霾污染法》因部分涉及火點的公司與新馬企業有關而難以有效執行；印尼民間團體則設立「氧氣小屋」，並對政府官員提起疏忽職守的集體訴訟。
summaryEn: This episode of What in the World examines how severe wildfires in Indonesia are spreading thick smog across Southeast Asia, heavily impacting air quality and daily life in Singapore and neighboring countries. Caused primarily by illegal 'slash and burn' land clearing and worsened by dry conditions from a Super El Niño, the fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan are the worst since 2015, resulting in over 170,000 acute respiratory infection cases in Indonesia. Smog has reduced visibility and led to school closures in Malaysia, while forcing Singaporeans to alter outdoor routines. BBC reporters Liza Tambunan in Indonesia and Tessa Wong in Singapore detail the responses: Singapore has opened community center refuge rooms and distributed masks, though enforcing its anti-haze laws remains tricky due to cross-border corporate links. Meanwhile, civil society groups in Indonesia have set up 'oxygen houses' and filed a class-action lawsuit against government officials for gross negligence.
